maintopic: U.S. TRADE EXPANSION ACT    MESSAGE FROM PRIME MINISTER

speechtext:
Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbalcer (Prime
Minister): Mr. Speaker, I sent a message to the President of the United States following the enactment of the trade expansion act, and instead of summarizing I think it would be appropriate if I were to read that message, containing as it does the views of the Canadian government in connection with the momentous step taken in the passage of that legislation. The message reads:
Dear Mr. President:
With the enactment of the trade expansion act I wish to let you know that the Canadian government welcomes this important development in United States trade policy which holds out promise for significant progress in the expansion of world trade on a multilateral basis. This is indeed an historic accomplishment.
At the commonwealth prime ministers' conference in London last month I proposed that all like-minded nations should meet at an early date to consider how the great problems of trade facing us today can be dealt with to the mutual advantage of all. I would like to follow up this general proposal with a specific suggestion for an early meeting on these matters. It is vitally important that we find effective ways as soon as possible for dealing with these complex and urgent trade problems. It appears that the most convenient way of arranging such a meeting would be to discuss these broad trade questions at a meeting of ministers.
The Canadian government looks forward to participating fully in these efforts and to working with the United States and other nations to achieve the objectives which we hold in common. It is our conviction that the opportunities now opened up for wider co-operation in trade and economic relations will make a major contribution to the further strengthening of the free world.
Trade relations between Canada and the United States are characterized by mutual understanding and a constructive approach to our common objective of freer, non-discriminatory trade. These new efforts to expand world trade will provide continuing opportunities for our two countries to work closely together each in a full understanding of the other's interests and aspirations.
Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the
Opposition): Mr. Speaker, the house will have listened with great interest to the statement of the Prime Minister in regard to the trade expansion program of the government of the United States, which has received the approval of congress. Mr. Speaker, we on this side have supported this proposal, in so far
as any persons outside the United States can support a program of this kind, since it was first introduced by the President as one of far reaching importance, both constructive and imaginative in its scope. It is indeed, as the Prime Minister has said, an historic accomplishment on the part of the administration of the United States. It is important for Canada and other countries to associate themselves with this kind of initiative so as to make sure that the step taken in Washington can be followed-indeed, preceded if possible -by steps taken in other free world capitals so that obstacles to trade can be removed in all free countries.
For that purpose, we have felt that the best move which Canada can make at this time is not to call a general conference of the kind indicated by the Prime Minister, which among other things would overlap a proposal made at the United Nations for that purpose, but to associate ourselves with the United States, the United Kingdom, and the economic community in Europe to reduce barriers and to extend the reduction of those barriers under the most favoured nation clause to all free countries.
Mr. Speaker, steps to this end can be taken through the machinery which is now available. It was interesting to note that at the Seigniory club yesterday the United States assistant secretary of state for economic affairs indicated that he felt the Canadian government could make a substantial contribution to freer trade by joining with the United States and other countries in working out a basis for negotiations on tariff reductions expected to begin before long. As he put it, Canada and the United States should be prepared to make short run adjustments for the sake of long term benefits.

maintopic: U.S. TRADE EXPANSION ACT    MESSAGE FROM PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is interesting to note, I think, that we who sit on the benches opposite the government have some measure of agreement on this particular statement which has just been made. However, we are convinced that the only way in which the freest possible exchange of goods among the nations of the world can be accomplished is by the lowering of tariff barriers. While we are also agreed that a world trade conference is of urgent importance, yet let us also remind ourselves- and I trust that the government is doing likewise-that we must start some place and do so soon. In this regard I think that the

Statement on U.S. Trade Expansion best instrument we have and likewise the best instrument which our neighbour to the south has is to be found in the relationship that must continue to develop between our two countries.
Again I come back to this factor, namely that one of the soundest bases for the beginning of what we understand to be a freer exchange of goods through the lowering of customs barriers, could well start within the commonwealth. After all, it must start some place. It is therefore our opinion that first with our neighbour to the south but immediately also within the realm of the commonwealth we must take action that will bring results in the immediate future. Unless we can free the restrictions that today limit the exchange of goods among friendly nations, we will not be able to meet the financial crisis we are in.
We are pleased that this step has been taken. However, again let us be practical in understanding that we must start some place and do so very soon.

maintopic: U.S. TRADE EXPANSION ACT    MESSAGE FROM PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Speaking for the New Democratic party, Mr. Speaker, may I say that we should like to associate ourselves with the words of the Prime Minister in welcoming the passage of the United States trade expansion act. As all hon. members know, this act is one of the most imaginative and far reaching to appear on the world scene for many years. It holds out the hope to all the free nations involved in it for a gradual lowering of trade barriers. It is the one weapon which may effectively be able to facilitate British entry into the European economic community and bring down the external tariff wall. It will also in all likelihood provide greatly renewed vigour and impetus for the coming trade negotiations under GATT in late 1963 and early 1964.
We hope the Canadian government will do everything in its power to bring our country under the provisions of the trade expansion act which deal with the 80 per cent figure, and will permit us to obtain free access to the United States and European markets. As I say, it is an imaginative and bold step. We in this party welcome it and urge the government to co-operate in every way.

STATEMENT BY MR. SPEAKER WITH REGARD TO QUESTIONS ON ORDERS OF THE DAY
speechtext: ['Agreed.']

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: STATEMENT BY MR. SPEAKER WITH REGARD TO QUESTIONS ON ORDERS OF THE DAY
speechtext:
Before calling the orders of the day I would crave the indulgence of hon. members in order to permit me to make a statement which I indicated on Friday last I would make today, namely a statement of what I consider to be the guideposts on the subject of questions generally and on oral questions on orders of the day in particular.
I would immediately point out that this is in no way a ruling but rather a statement.
I find that over the past 20 years or more each of my predecessors as Speaker has taken this step I am now taking at least once, and some of them a number of times, during his term of office.
The problem of oral questions on orders of the day is not a new one and hon. members will see some of the reasons why as we examine the problem. As there are a number of hon. members who were members of this house in 1940 perhaps I could quote from some observations by the then prime minister, Mr. Mackenzie King, as they appear in Hansard for July 12, 1940, commencing at page 1569:
It is not, as I understand the rules, the right of hon. members to interrogate the ministry upon all kinds of matters without advance notice and without following, wherever possible, the other rules that are laid down for the seeking and obtaining of information. The rules of the house do provide several means whereby information may be obtained, and of course the rule most generally availed of is the one with respect to handing questions in to the clerk, or having placed on the order paper notices of motions for the production of papers. By our rules the asking of questions of the ministry on the orders of the day is limited to a certain class of questions, those which cannot be answered effectively in the other way.
He further indicated he felt the Speaker of the day should make a statement in this regard. Mr. Speaker Glen on July 15, 1940, as reported on page 1596 of Hansard, went into the question at some length and, after reading standing order 44, comparable to our standing order 39 of today, had this to say:
If the standing order was strictly interpreted, it is obvious that a very large proportion of the oral questions asked before orders of the day are called would be out of order. In fact, members have not exercised sufficiently their rights under standing order 44, but have too frequently endeavoured to seek information on the orders of the day being called.
He went on further to say, on pages 1596 and 1597:
To sum up: There is only one standing order governing questions seeking information from ministers of the crown. It is standing order 44, which provides that such questions may be marked with an asterisk if oral answers are required. Forty-eight hours' notice must be given of these questions, which must be laid on the table of the house before six o'clock

and printed in the Votes and Proceedings. On the orders of the day being called, members may ask ministers to explain certain matters in accordance with the practice expounded by Bourinot and sanctioned by usage. It is not done under the authority of a standing order, and therefore such questions may be either permitted or disallowed by the Speaker, who must judge each case on its merits.
And further:
... It seems to me manifestly unfair to compel ministers to answer questions on important matters without an opportunity of consulting their chief officers; and it would be arbitrary to deprive private members of the privilege of putting certain questions of immediate urgency on the orders of the day being called. The principle on which the practice has been tolerated in past years should be respected, that is, the reading of long series of questions elaborately prepared is not to be allowed on the orders of the day being called.
Again, on March 15, 1943, as reported at page 1234 of Hansard, Mr. Speaker Glen had this to say:
As long as our standing orders are unchanged, the only questions permitted on the orders of the day being called must be confined to very urgent matters, personal explanations, inaccurate reports of speeches delivered in the house, denial of charges, dilatoriness in obtaining returns, or other similar matters closely connected with the routine business of the house. These questions must be brief and must not be prefaced by any argument. Standing order 44 gives members ample opportunity to place on the order paper any number of questions they desire with respect to public affairs. Reading telegrams, letters or extracts from newspapers as an opening to a question when the orders of the day are called is an abuse of the rules of the house. It is not good parliamentary practice to communicate written allegations to the house and then to ask ministers either to confirm or to deny them. It is the member's duty to ascertain the truth of any statement before he brings it to the attention of parliament. This has been decided long ago in the United Kingdom House of Commons. On June 14, 1882, Mr. Speaker Brand, in preventing a member from reading a telegram from a newspaper and founding a question on it, pointed out the extreme inconvenience of founding questions on every telegram in every newspaper. "I am bound to say," he added, ''that it does appear to me that before questions of such gravity are put, an hon. member should take some measures to ascertain the truth of the telegram." This quotation is from Denison's and Brand's Decisions, page 230.
Mr. Speaker Glen concluded as follows:
I feel it is my duty to explain to the house the procedure with regard to questions, and I hope that in applying it I shall have the co-operation of all members of the house.
On September 11, 1945, page 66 of Hansard, Mr. Speaker Fauteux had this to say briefly after citing Beauchesne's third edition:
Hon. members will notice that the rules say that questions are allowed by courtesy in connection with the business of the house, or with very urgent and important matters of public concern. I would like to call for the co-operation of every member and ask them not to put oral questions when they are not very urgent. It would be preferable for the dispatch of business that questions be placed on the order paper.
Coming to more recent years, on May 29, 1951, as reported in Hansard, page 3494, Mr. Statement by Mr. Speaker Speaker Macdonald referred to the procedure regarding the asking of questions, and he referred hon. members to standing order 44 I quote:
It has nevertheless been the practice in our house to allow a certain number of oral questions, and it is not my purpose to discourage members from asking questions of the proper type, as I feel that these questions create a more lively interest in the business of the house. These oral questions are asked when the orders of the day are called, and are frequently asked without notice. I would, however, emphasize that these oral questions should be asked only in connection with very urgent and important matters of public concern, and only if it would not be in the public interest to place them on the order paper and receive answers in accordance with the method provided for in the standing orders. They should always be brief. No debate is permitted, and the reply should be as concise as possible. The questions should not be prefaced by the reading of letters, telegrams, newspaper extracts or preambles of any kind. See Beauchesne's third edition, paragraphs 297, 298.
On March 16, 1956, Mr. Speaker Beaudoin, as reported on page 2206 to 2210' of Hansard and the Journals of the House of Commons, volume C. at pages 299 and those following went into the whole question most exhaustively. He reviewed the statements of the previous Speakers, including some of those which I have given to hon. members, and then cited from other sources of authority such as Beauchesne, Bourinot and May as well as articles published by the Hansard Society. Without appearing at all to lecture hon. members in a pedagogic way, I would suggest that this particular statement by Mr. Speaker Beaudoin might be made prescribed reading for members, as well as others who would comment upon the proceedings of this house.
The statement came relatively shortly after standing orders had been changed and adopted by the house in 1955, following many years of study. There are many hon. members on both sides of this house who were members of the House of Commons in 1955 and who participated in the revision of the standing orders and, with the adoption of the standing orders, I may presume that they concurred therein.
I am resisting a grave temptation to quote most extensively from this lengthy statement, and I trust that hon. members will bear with me while I make certain references to it. In some respects the situation today may resemble that which prevailed some six years ago:
I want to tell hon. members that I think that between their conception of what should be asked at question time and mine there is now such a wide difference that I am afraid we are not pulling in the same direction. I think it is well for me to establish the position which I consider is the one which is now in force. I will not quote all these citations but I will refer hon. members to the following ones-

Statement by Mr. Speaker
Then he enumerates a number from Beau-chesne. He refers members to Bourinot's fourth edition and goes on and cites particularly citation 140 in Beauchesne's third edition, which is as follows:
A question which could be inserted on the order paper is not allowed on the orders of the day being called.
Incidentally, citation 140 is now 173, subparagraph 2:
Then citation 297:
297. A certain number of oral questions are permitted in practice by members, without notice, before the orders of the day are called; but these are merely allowed by courtesy in connection with the business of the house or with very urgent and important matters of public concern. They are always brief, no debate being permitted, and the replies are as concise as possible. The minister interrogated may reply at once or may direct that the usual notice be given. Such questions are governed by the same rules of order as questions of which notice has been given.
Then Mr. Speaker Beaudoin comments:
In other words, if a question could not be inserted on the order paper, a member cannot ask it before the orders of the day are called.
There follows some detailed discussion and interpretation of various citations in Beau-chesne, which I do not think it is necessary to deal with at this time, but in case this statement should be misunderstood in regard to citation 203 of the third edition of Beauchesne, which is now citation 178 of the fourth edition, it must be noted that Mr. Speaker Beaudoin subsequently corrected himself on May 7, 1956 as reported in volume 4 of Hansard at pages 3619 and 3620. Mr. Speaker Beaudoin then continued, at the foot of page 2207 of Hansard:
I hope that hon. members will read carefully all the citations I have given and I feel confident that they will do so knowing their interest in the matter. They will see that not only has it been the opinion of prime ministers but also of leaders of the opposition when they have occupied one side or the other during their careers, that questions before the orders of the day are called should be limited to questions of an urgent and important character and should be asked on the orders of the day only if they could not be placed on the order paper without some prejudice being suffered.
I said earlier that hon. members are moving in a direction which is contrary to that which I understand to be the right one because as hon. members know the rules are not being changed by the Speaker. If hon. members wish that the rules be changed there is a proper method to be adopted and that is to have a committee on rules, have the matter decided and have a report made to the house. Were I to receive such a report I can assure you that I would try to interpret the new rules as faithfully as I could. As it is, hon. members are trying to move in the direction of having a question period which is almost similar to that which exists in the United Kingdom without adopting the proper safeguards and without giving more authority to the Speaker to intervene whenever he feels that a question is not in order and also without adopting the method of giving notice which is in vogue in the United Kingdom.

He then went on to compare the practice which prevails in the United Kingdom, which is quite instructive. I cannot resist reference to a citation made by Mr. Speaker Beaudoin from a commentary on "Question time in Canada" appearing in an article of the Hansard Society, where the author has this to say:
In Canada, the complexity of the question procedure and its lack of definitiveness usually results in an annual altercation on the floor of the house.
I think hon. members who have been here for some time may be witness to that. Then he says:
Habitually, Mr. Speaker makes a short statement-
And, as Mr. Speaker Beaudoin does, I apologize for making mine quite so long:
-during the early stages of the parliamentary session to remind the members of the differences between the two procedures to be outlined below. The Speaker tries to discourage the use of too many questions being asked "on the orders of the day being called''.
Even closer to the present day, with respect I would refer to two statements made by my immediate predecessor, Mr. Speaker Michener, on October 17, 1957, at page 63 of Hansard, where the then Speaker referred hon. members directly to the lengthy statement by his immediate predecessor, Mr. Speaker Beaudoin, and it is my opinion that Mr. Speaker Michener adopted the words of Mr. Speaker Beaudoin.
Again on February 26, 1959 at page 1393 of Hansard, Mr. Speaker Michener on an occasion similar to this, prior to calling orders of the day, made a statement as to the interpretation of the practice of this house on oral questions for the edification of hon. members; and without wishing to enter into debate with anyone within or without this house who may feel that I am endeavouring to introduce changes in the rules or interpretations of the rules concerning oral questions, may I quote the principles applicable to oral questions as enumerated briefly by Mr. Speaker Michener.
1.	The question should seek information or press for action on a matter relating to public affairs of such immediate urgency that it would be inappropriate to put it on the order paper.
2.	Both the question and the answer should be concise, factual and free of opinion and argument or observations which might lead to debate.
3.	An explanation can be sought regarding the intention of the government but not an explanation of opinion upon matters of policy. That is citation 178 of Beauchesne's fourth edition.
4.	Other detailed limitations, some 40 in number, are set out in citation 171 of Beauchesne's fourth edition ... and apply to oral questions as well as to written questions.
5.	Supplementary questions are matters of grace.
6.	The minister is entitled to notice, and answers cannot be insisted on nor is it regular to comment on the refusal to answer an oral question.

I may say this principle relates to oral questions and perhaps not to questions on the order paper.
I apologize to hon. members for the length of this statement which, if I had yielded to temptation, could have been much longer; but I felt it was necessary to trace an historical pattern to events which have taken place within the actual memory of a goodly number of hon. members in this house. Unfortunately human memory may sometimes fail or impressions may get blurred of events even not too distant in the past, but the Journals of this house and the records of debates indicate faithfully what was actually said. I leave it to hon. members to judge my submission that there is an easily discernible line of interpretation over the years, but one must refresh one's memory from time to time to clearly set out and see that line of interpretation.
I do not propose to enter into a lengthy philosophical dissertation on the role of the Speaker, his duties having been described much better by others on many occasions. I would subscribe wholeheartedly to those definitions. I believe the Speaker should be the impartial arbiter of the rules as they exist for him and for the house in the standing orders, in the decisions of his predecessors and in the decisions of this house, aided by the persuasive authority of the commentaries such as Beauchesne, Bourinot, May and others. The Speaker is the servant of the house in so far as it makes rules for the conduct of its affairs, and I conceive it would be a grave dereliction of duty for the Speaker to put these rules aside consciously in response to either whim or expediency.
But if the rules exist for the Speaker to interpret, they also exist for hon. members to observe. It is not the sole duty of the Speaker to preserve order, or the traditions and dignity of this house, or to protect members from unconscionable actions. I would submit that there is an equal duty on all members to do likewise. May I translate ourselves into another medium which may be more graphic. The rule book does not exist only for the hockey referee or the football referee or the umpire in baseball, nor are these officials the only ones who should know the book of rules; the players themselves, if they are going to do their jobs properly, must not only know the rules well but must observe them.
I do not conceive the role of Speaker to be that of a police constable on a beat in a more notorious section of a large metropolitan city, whose principal task is to be on constant alert against wrongdoings and where the conduct of most of the residents may be suspect. Nor do I conceive it to be that of a mere teller of names, a sort of gatekeeper for hon. members
Statement by Mr. Speaker who may wish to ask questions or engage in debate governed by the rules of this house to the extent only that the whim or the expediency of the moment may dictate. I recognize that these are extreme positions.
As I have indicated previously, and as has been indicated by previous Speakers, I have my rules as embodied in standing orders, decisions of this house, decisions of previous Speakers and the persuasive authority of the commentaries. Hon. members expect me to enforce these rules; yet, as was said by Mr. Speaker Beaudoin, "It would appear that hon. members are pulling in the direction of the practice which exists in the United Kingdom under different rules." If the present rules do not satisfy the hon. members of this house, then I have no objection if they wish to go in different directions, but I cannot agree that I can go along with them while following the rules which are given to me. If the rules should be changed, then I respectfully suggest that hon. members know what procedure to take under the rules as they now exist.
May I add that many of the questions being posed on orders of the day would be unacceptable as to form for printing on the notice paper. In a large percentage of such cases members would be requested to rephrase or redraft their notices before they could be accepted under the terms of standing order 39, section 1.
In conclusion, briefly stated, it would appear that it has been the consensus of all Speakers that questions asked on orders of the day should comply with two basic requirements:
1.	The form of those questions is governed by the terms of standing order 39 section 1, which provides in part that in putting a question no argument or opinion is to be offered nor any facts stated except so far as might be necessary to explain the question.
2.	Such questions should be offered only in connection with urgent and important matters of public concern when, because of immediacy, the regular procedure relating to questions cannot be utilized for the purpose of eliciting the desired information or for bringing a matter of urgency to the attention of the ministry.
The terms of section 1 of standing order 39 are comparatively clear, and if the Chair could depend on co-operation from all sides of the house not only as to the nature of questions but also as to the nature of replies, there would be little trouble, in my humble opinion, in controlling questions on orders of the day.
I respectfully submit this statement for the consideration of hon. members.

In so far as Berlin is concerned, western policy has not changed in spite of the fact that there have been some indications that the Soviet union may shortly precipitate a new, if not a grave, crisis in that city. The basic essentials of western policy are the maintenance of allied rights on access, the continuing presence of western troops and the freedom of the people of western Berlin. The house resumed, from Monday, October 15, consideration in committee of Bill No. C-63, to amend the Export Credits Insurance Act-Mr. Hees-Mr. Chown in the chair.
On clause 3-Power to lend or guarantee, etc.

Before the clause is carried I should like to pose a question to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, if I could have his attention, and in the light of his reply to pose a second question, but the second question depends upon his reply to the first. The answer is no, Mr. Chairman.
Could I ask the minister if he is completely satisfied with the competence of the officials and the conscientious way in which they carry out their duties?
The answer is yes.

Then I wonder if the Minister of Trade and Commerce can explain to us what he meant when he said last night, as recorded on page 557 of Hansard:
I was most interested to hear the hon. member for Ottawa West harking back to what he would consider the good old days, the 22 years when patronage really ran rampant.
Of course this corporation has only existed 17 years, but we will pardon the minister his bad arithmetic.
From listening to him talk, you would think we were doing the kind of things that happened when they were in power, when deals were made-
The minister was speaking of this corporation.
-with specific firms that were friendly and so on That is something that does not happen any more
After an interruption the minister went on to say:
I wish to tell hon. members that it was made very clear to all Canadian producers that any terms which are made available to any one producer are available to all producers of that commodity. I know the hon. member is amazed to hear that statement, as that sort of thing never happened during the 22 years during which his party was in power. However, it happens now and it has happened under this government ever since we took over office and cleaned things up five years ago.

Export Credits Insurance Act
I have a couple of questions I want to put to the minister, and I hope he will be able to answer them instead of making another cheap political speech.
Oh, oh.
I have been reading his cheap political speech, not making one myself.
You are doing a pretty good job yourself.

I should like to ask the
minister to tell us precisely what he did to clean up this corporation that he has said was so unsatisfactory during the previous regime. I also think the minister, having made that broad statement, should give us the names of those firms that were specially favoured and are favoured no more.

Mr. Chairman, this is a very easy and very pleasant thing to do. I was not, of course, referring to the operations of the corporation. I was referring to the operations of the government as they took place under section 21. Ever since the corporation was set up in 1944 and began to operate, insurance has been issued under section 14 on all commodities where the operation which it was desired to insure was of a regular nature. However, under section 21 requests for insurance had to be referred by the corporation to the governor in council because the terms of the operation which it was desired to insure went beyond what the corporation considered to be the normal manner of carrying on its business. Therefore under section 21, both under the last government and the present one, these matters have been referred to the governor in council for consideration to see whether or not the insurance requested should be approved. Under the present government it has always been our practice to consider these matters on a businesslike basis, and any terms that we make available to any one corporation are, of course, available to any other corporation.
What I was referring to were the decisions made by the previous government in the old days, and the way they handled business generally during their 22 years in office, in that they often decided they would carry out certain transactions not necessarily on the basis of business considerations but on whether or not certain friends of theirs appealed to them from time to time and asked for special consideration. That is what I was referring to last night. In no way, of course, was I criticizing the operations of the corporation as such; rather I was criticizing the business philosophy of the late Liberal government as it operated during its 22 years of mismanagement in this country.

The hon. gentleman has made charges of a general nature against a man who was highly respected in this country and is now dead. I ask the minister to give specific examples of these things. I suggest that he either withdraw these imputations or that he produce the evidence on which he makes these airy-fairy charges. I suggest, too, that the hon. gentleman stop inflating himself to try to look like C. D. Howe.
Mr. C. D. Howe was one member of the former government for whom I always had great respect, and in anything I said about the former government I was certainly not referring to Mr. Howe.
He was the minister concerned.
As the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate knows, one member of the cabinet does not decide government policy. I was referring to the operations of the government as a whole.

I have listened to some of the remarks that have been made within the last few minutes, and I am more convinced than ever that we spend more time in political manoeuvring and back-talk in this house than we do in constructive debate. Let us get on with it. I believe the mark of an intelligent man is that he can, with the least words, say something constructive. According to what we hear, we are not out of the kindergarten yet. I suggest that since we have more or less agreed on the basic principles involved, we should get through with it and move on to something else.
I should like to take just one minute, Mr. Chairman, to correct a statement that was made yesterday concerning wheat exports. In checking the Bank of Canada's statistical summary for 1961, page 152, and using my addition pencil, I find that during the years 1952 through 1956 we exported $2,868 million of wheat, and wheat flour, and in the years 1957 to 1961 the figure was 2,660 million; for total grain, it is 3,665 million bushels in the first five years, and 3,051 million in the last five years. I just wanted to correct that for the sake of the record.

Since the hon. gentleman has chosen, in making a correction, to make an imputation about what other hon. members said, particularly referring to me and to the minister, since we were the only two who had spoken, I suggest to the hon. member for Red Deer that it is just as important to protect the reputation of a man who served his country well in this parliament for a

great many years, and whose reputation is attacked by his successor, as it is to make a correction in a little arithmetic.
Order.

Just to keep the record straight,
1	should like to repeat that I was in no way attacking the late Right Hon. C. D. Howe, for whom I had great respect. I was talking of the government.
You don't know what you are talking about.

I should like to ask the minister two or three questions, of which I have sent him notice. How much actual money will be held by the authority, the Export Credits Insurance Corporation, in connection with the $400 million, the $300 million and the $200 million? How much interest is paid by those using this credit? What is the source of the funds used by the Export Credits Insurance Corporation, and what is the source of the funds to pay the expenses of the corporation?

The answer is that the Export Credits Insurance Corporation holds no money at all for its operations under section 14 or section 21, other than the capital which was originally prescribed and which it holds and uses for the purpose of paying claims whenever such payments are necessary.

I want to clear up a point with which I sought to deal when the particular question was before the committee. The minister, in his remarks as reported on page 557 of Hansard, was dealing with section 21 of the act as it is being amended by clause
2	of this bill. This section comes directly under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Trade and Commerce; it is his ministerial responsibility. His remarks, therefore, are capable of one interpretation and one only, and that is that the minister, who represents the government and speaks for the government in these matters, is the one about whom he was speaking. In this case it could only mean the late Right Hon. C. D. Howe.
Furthermore, I would point out that his remarks are capable of one interpretation only in addition, that is that certain firms in this country improperly received benefit under this legislation. Now the minister, having cast that aspersion on these firms, has an obligation to explain to the committee just what firms he had in mind, who they were, and either withdraw the smear on them or substantiate it by evidence.
Before he does that I would point out that a great number of the transactions to which he referred were transactions involving sales by the Canadian wheat board. I was amazed 27507-3-37
Export Credits Insurance Act to note the applause that came from government supporters from the three prairie provinces, the wheat country, at the minister's remark presumably indicating favouritism shown to the wheat board.
I am sure the minister spoke too hastily and without thinking through his remarks. If that is the case, I do wish he would clear it up and withdraw; because I am sure, as Minister of Trade and Commerce, it is not desirable that he be in the position of having cast such a reflection on either the commercial firms in the country or the Canadian wheat board.

I am very glad to say that I cast no reflection on anyone except the late lamented Liberal government. As the hon. member knows very well, under section 21 the Minister of Trade and Commerce brings forward applications to the council and the council decides whether or not the insurance requested by the producer shall be granted. It is not the sole responsibility of the minister by any manner of means. He merely brings the request forward, and the cabinet decide that they will or will not grant the insurance being requested in that particular case. In no way at all, therefore, was I referring specifically to the late Right Hon. C. D. Howe for whom, I say a third time, I had great respect. I was in no way referring to him, but I referred to the government as a whole.
The way in which my remark came about last night was that the hon. member for Ottawa West was thinking of the way the government used to operate in the old days under the patronage system, and he said that the use of section 21 opens up the possibility for patronage in a very big way. I simply remarked that the hon. member must be thinking back to the way his government operated for 22 years in all fields. I, of course, was making no allegation against any specific firm. He knows that quite well.

Last night I brought to the attention of the committee and the minister a legal objection to some of the terminology used in the proposed amendment to section 21(a) 2 (e) and section 21(a) 6(b). The words in question to which I referred are "interest in any such instrument". The objection I brought forward at that time was that the instrument in question is a negotiable instrument and is transferable with all the interest in it or is not transferable at all. It is not severable. The minister subsequently advised me of the government's intention in this amendment, which was apparently to refer to a common banking practice whereby a contract can be entered into between the

Export Credits Insurance Act corporation and a commercial bank and, tor a consideration, give the commercial bank participation in the instrument.
I should like to suggest to the minister that the section might be further amended to extend the powers of the corporation so as to give the corporation the power to exchange any guaranteed instrument for two or more instruments of lesser principal amount, aggregating the amount of the original instrument, and to sell all or any part of such instruments. The minister is aware of a recent negotiation under this statute which provided for the refunding of obligations which had previously been created, and I should like to recommend to him the possibility of incorporating in the powers of the corporation this further power so that if it becomes commercially feasible the corporation may sell some of its obligations on the public money market or to private purchasers. My submission is that the wording at the present time does not give the corporation this power, and being a statutory corporation it is strictly limited to the powers conferred under the statute. Therefore I would propose that amendment to the minister.

Mr. Chairman, I thank the hon. member for Rosedale for his thoughtful suggestion. I have discussed this matter with the officers of the Export Credits Insurance Corporation and they consider that the powers which will be conferred upon them by this amendment provide them with the widest possible powers they could need. What is being done here is making it possible for our corporation to operate in exactly the same manner as the export-import bank of the United States, which handles these matters in the same way as we do. The officers of the corporation are of the opinion that this amendment will give them the fullest possible powers that they could need.

Mr. Chairman, my decision to participate in this debate was prompted by the political tirade that we received from the minister yesterday afternoon. speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. If there are hon. members who intend to leave the chamber,, may they do so with dispatch and a certain degree of quiet so that the hon. member from Winnipeg North may be heard without undue delay.

More and more people are finding it impossible to meet payments for purchases made on instalments and are going broke in the process. The old adages we used to hear preached so often about careful management, thrift, and buying only what we can afford have practically disappeared from the Canadian language except, of course, where applied by some stump speakers to government operations. Few people in Canada can ignore the siren calls of the advertisers designed to make us all want to keep up with the Joneses. It is practically a sin if we do not own our home, drive a car or possess a television set, an automatic washing machine or a dryer. Even if we cannot really afford these things we have got to have them. After all, it is easy to charge now and pay later or, as the air lines advertise so effectively, travel now and pay later. And if some people do not know how to get credit, there are plenty of retailers and friendly finance companies who will show them how to do it with a simple stroke of a pen.
Later, many people find it is difficult or impossible to meet the supposedly easy payments; but by then it is too late, the borrower is in trouble. He finds out, then, that he is not nearly as popular as he was, or thought he was, when he was buying. He finds out that he is just a small cog in the wheel, just a statistic. He finds out that the retail store which encouraged him to buy the stove or the washing machine or the television set, and which did not ask too many questions about how many other things he was buying at the same time, or whether he could afford to pay for them or not, wants its money. What is more likely, and even worse, is that the finance company to which the retail store

sold the note wants the money and wants it right away. The borrower is on his own. It is then he gets the nasty telephone calls, the threatening letters, the judgment summons, the garnishee order and all the rest of it. This is the time when the creditor stops answering the telephone; when he stops answering the ring of the doorbell and pulls down the blinds of the front room so that people will think he is not at home. But, of course, by that time it is too late. This is when employers often fire employees because they do not like to be involved in the kind of squeeze represented by garnishee orders. By this time many people are so far in debt that they cannot manage to work their way out in the time allotted to them.
This bill uses the present machinery of the Bankruptcy Act and the bankruptcy courts to protect both the wage earner in trouble and his creditor. The legitimate creditor is entitled to protection. The bill offers an inexpensive procedure by means of which the wage earner can pay his creditors.
Under this bill a new part is added to the Bankruptcy Act following section 26 of the act. This permits an insolvent wage earner to make an assignment to an official receiver who has the power to appoint a trustee to handle the case. The wage earner is obliged to submit his future wages to the trustee's control, so that the trustee may make regular payments to the wage earner's creditors.
The trustee can apply to the bankruptcy court for relief of the wage earner against unconscionable contracts, and the court has the power to exempt the wage earner from payment of excessive interest charges of which there are far too many.
The court has the power to enforce obedience to the arrangements worked out by the trustee. The court has the power to discharge the wage earner when he has fulfilled his obligations under the proposal. If the debts have not been paid off after three years, the wage earner must apply to the court for an extension of time in which to do so.
This bill would help both wage earner and creditor. The wage earner would be aided in the orderly payment of his debts, and the creditor would be more likely to get the money which he has loaned to the wage earner, usually in the form of goods sold.
Mr. Speaker, similar bills have been enacted in the United States and have helped thousands of creditors there. This bill would prevent financial ruin for many people and deserves the support of all hon. members.

Mr. Speaker, the general idea behind this bill is commendable. There has long been 27507-3-38
Bankruptcy Act
a need in this country for legislation of this kind which will simplify the procedure for people who are not in business and to whom the bankruptcy legislation does not presently apply. These are people who want to make an arrangement of some kind with their creditors but do not have the assets or the ability to proceed under the Bankruptcy Act as it presently stands.
Legislation similar to this particular bill has already been introduced into other legislative bodies, as has been said by the hon. member who introduced the bill. Specifically in Canada there was a bill in the province of Alberta which was passed in 1959 and had similar objectives, but was a much different bill. This bill was the orderly payment of debts act of 1959 of the province of Alberta. That legislation was passed in order to permit debtors who wanted to make an assignment or an arrangement with their creditors to do so. The Supreme Court of Canada ruled in 1960 that the measure was invalid because it infringed on the powers of the federal parliament to make bankruptcy laws. This decision is reported in 1960 Supreme Court Reports, page 571. The supreme court held that, although there may have been some provincial rights involved, the legislation which the province of Alberta had passed was in substance bankruptcy legislation and therefore beyond the power of a provincial legislature.
Following this declaration, of course, it is obvious that the power to pass such legislation rests solely within the parliament of Canada, and this legislation now proposed appears to be quite in order from the constitutional viewpoint. Although the bill is not yet before us, Mr. Speaker, I think we should take note of the fact that in the other place the government has already introduced legislation of a similar type, and it is to be found in Bill S-2 of the Senate. I would not want to discuss this bill because it has not yet come before us, but I think we should take note of the fact that there is similar legislation proposed, although somewhat different in form and content, to the bill we are now discussing.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to point out a few matters which are deficiencies in the bill which is now presented to us. The bill we have before us is applicable only to persons classified as wage earners, and I believe there are others who should also be covered by this legislation. I think it could very well be extended to include anyone who is not normally included in the present bankruptcy legislation. The present legislation makes provision for companies, and persons carrying on a trade or business, to go into bankruptcy, but it does not make provision

Bankruptcy Act
for the private individual. I think this bill would be improved if it were expanded to include any private person, not just an individual wage earner as defined in the bill.
I think there is a second deficiency we should look at very carefully, and this is that under Bill No. C-7, the wage earner has to go into bankruptcy before he can get the protection or the benefit of the act. I think there should be a simplified way of allowing debtors to make a compromise or consolidation of debts other than by going into bankruptcy. I feel that the wording of clause 26(b), although we are not permitted to discuss it, indicates that the wage earner must have filed an assignment, and therefore at that point he would be a bankrupt; and if he had the ability in subsequent years to pay off his debts bit by bit and finally get released, in the meantime he would have been classified a bankrupt even if his debts were not large and he was asking merely for an extension.
There are a couple of other things I should likewise mention. The most difficult part of this bill, I believe, is the clause which allows a trustee to apply to the courts to modify existing contracts. This particular clause is a most difficult one, particularly from the constitutional aspect, because contracts are certainly property and civil rights, and normally come within the jurisdiction of the province. However, the supreme court might very well hold that, if it were ancillary to bankruptcy legislation, it would be valid. But we have another matter to consider, a moral matter rather than a legal or constitutional one, and that is whether we should allow a court or a trustee to alter an existing contract. We know that such a course has recently been followed in certain provincial legislation, in which contracts which were binding were permitted to be altered. But contracts generally are considered to be sacred once they are signed by parties who know what they are doing when they sign them. Any other type of contract which is fraudulent can be declared void by the courts and set aside. But I believe we are entering into a very dangerous field, Mr. Speaker, in the particular clause of this bill which permits the court to revise a contract already signed and in force at the time the trustee takes over. I think that is a very difficult matter and that the clause as it presently stands does not contain the proper safeguards that we should like to have in connection with the validity and sacredness of contracts properly signed. This particular clause causes me some considerable difficulty.
I would also suggest to the hon. member that the bill is not clear as to whether or not debts have to be paid in full before a debtor can obtain a discharge. The notes in connection with the bill indicate that they must be,

but the bill itself is not clear. There is provision for the discharge of a person who has lived up to whatever is provided for. I think the bill could be improved considerably were it made more clear whether or not debts must be paid up in full before a discharge could be received.
There is one other difficulty which I can see in the bill as it stands at present. It relates to the provision that all other sections of the Bankruptcy Act shall apply to this amendment. The Bankruptcy Act is an extremely complicated and difficult statute, of course. It contains provisions which apply to large bankruptcies or to persons who have extremely large debts. It may be the case that there are a great many sections of the Bankruptcy Act which should not apply. The difficulty with regard to this type of legislation was pointed out in a case in the Ontario supreme court. It was styled as Be W. Hanna Company and is found in Canadian Bankruptcy Reports 1961, volume 2, at page 70. In that particular case a proposal under the Bankruptcy Act was being considered and it was found most difficult to apply all the provisions of the Bankruptcy Act to proposals. I believe the present bill is one further extension of the proposals which at present are in the bill. Hence in this particular case I think it would be much better if there were a more detailed spelling out of the provisions of the Bankruptcy Act which should apply to wage earners.
Notwithstanding the criticisms I have made, Mr. Speaker, the principle behind the bill is a good one. I believe the principle of Bill No. S-2 which may in due course come before us should be left open, and that we should consider this Senate bill when it comes here, prior to making a final decision on Bill No. C-7 which is now before us. I believe the major difficulty is that the debtor himself must go into bankruptcy. I think there should be a provision which would allow him merely to consolidate his debts and to make a proposal to his creditors which would be sanctioned by the courts and by law, without the need of going into bankruptcy.
There is in the bill a provision that the trustee shall be appointed without being bonded and that any person other than a licensed trustee can be appointed. I believe this is a rather dangerous procedure. I realize that it is necessary to make provisions under which it will be easy for the debtor to make an application under this act. However, to make an application to any person, whether a licensed trustee or not or whether bonded or not, I believe is a rather dangerous proposal. In the result, Mr. Speaker, while I commend the principle of the bill, I would prefer that we do not make a final decision on

it until amendments could be made in order to bring it into conformity with some of the suggestions I have made, and perhaps until after we have had an opportunity to consider Bill No. S-2 which no doubt will in due course come to us from the other place.
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) is to be commended-

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext: The hon. member means the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow).

Yes, the hon. member for Winnipeg North. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre is on his feet so often in the house that one can probably be given some consideration and understanding with regard to errors that are made. The hon. member rises quite frequently, to his credit I must admit.
This bill now before us is one that takes into consideration the serious financial situation in which an individual wage earner or other individual may find himself through over-extending his credit. The hon. member has pointed out the many inducements that are put before the buying public in these days of mass production and as an indication that it is becoming more widespread and that there should be some legislation which would assist the individual as opposed to the corporation, has referred to the fact that even the chartered banks have now gone into the consumer credit business. However, there is one thing which we must bear in mind, namely that the creditor, in extending credit, will with respect to each application give consideration to the trustworthiness of - the applicant. As we constrict the collecting possibilities or, for that matter, in many instances the interest rates, we narrow the field in which the applicant may be able to obtain necessary financing under circumstances that may be extremely urgent. For that reason I think we should be careful that we do not, by enacting too many measures, restrict the ability of the individual to obtain cash when it is required.
I was unable to hear the hon. member too well when he was speaking and I am not sure whether he referred to the Lacombe act which is in effect in the province of Quebec. This act seems to work successfully, I have been told, in that a person who finds himself in circumstances of imminent bankruptcy may apply to the court for permission to consolidate his debts and to make restitution on a monthly basis as a percentage of his salary. The hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka has indicated that such an act was declared to be ultra vires the powers 27507-3-38)
Bankruptcy Act
of the provinces in respect of the province of Alberta. There must therefore be some difference in the two acts to which I am referring. It might be possible that this matter could be given consideration by the various provinces.
We believe that the principle of this measure is worthy of the consideration of the house. I as a member on this side of the house would not wish to delay action of the house. For that reason I think any further discussion by me on the matter is perhaps superfluous.

Mr. Speaker, first, I should like to make an observation. A while ago, I heard a member from which constituency I do not know, mention that similar legislation had been passed in Alberta only to be found ultra vires by the supreme court.
Well, I must say, Mr. Speaker, it does not mean that the legislation is bad, because, in Alberta, the Social Credit government tried some time ago to have seven pieces of legislation concerning money and provincial banks adopted, and they were all rejected by the privy council in London. Yet, they were the best ever put forward either by a provincial government or a federal government.
Mr. Speaker, when one reads the bill now before the house, one cannot fail to see how good it is, especially when it is seeking to protect the consumer from the excessive practices of the finance companies, which are only thinking of taking advantage of the consumer and getting rich at his expense.
Right now, I just happen to have, in the riding of Lapointe and in the whole Saguenay area, an example of consumers who have been taken in by finance companies and sewing machine salesmen. More than 80 people bought sewing machines or rather, were supposed to get them free. But before receiving them, they were asked to sign a financing contract, after which the selling firm agreed to make the monthly payments.
The selling firm discounted all contracts and notes through a finance company, the Seaboard Finance, and did not continue to make payments on behalf of the buyers. Today, those customers who got their sewing machines free have to pay them double their value.
If this Bill No. C-7 carried, the contracts would have to be revised so that the customers would not have to pay double the normal selling price simply because of a salesmanship scheme.

Bankruptcy Act
I think this bill would also provide a protection for the consumers who, in many cases, because we have tight money, must use finance plans to get what they need or else do without it. Very often the consumer has to borrow from some finance company to buy living room or bedroom furniture and then he may be out of work because that is a consequence of our present system. He may wish to buy a house with a repayment period of 25 years, but even then, he may happen to lose his job.
When that happens, the finance companies never lose, they repossess the articles, refrigerators, electrical stoves or furniture and then, the consumer loses not only the amounts he has already paid, but he is also deprived of what he had bought by the finance company which manages to resell those articles to friends, at a price much lower than the ordinary sale price. The finance company has the right to sue for the balance, that is the difference between the sale price and the instalments the first purchaser could not make.
Those are, Mr. Speaker, the situations in which the Canadian consumers find themselves. I could give you so many instances where it is always the little man who is crushed by the big finance companies. However, if one goes to the heart of the matter, one finds that in most cases those finance companies are branches of chartered banks which, finding that they do not make enough money when they make loans at 6 per cent, subsidize finance companies which make loans at interest rates of up to 24, 28 and even 32 per cent.
I know what I am talking about, Mr. Speaker, because in order to buy my car which is parked near the parliament buildings, I had to pay an interest rate of 32 per cent.
Then, the finance companies are subsidized or assisted by the chartered banks which are used to take unfair advantage of the small wage earner who is always facing great difficulties and paying more than others because he does not have the purchasing power with which to buy our goods.
You are not the only one who has to pay for his car through a finance company.

No, I am not the only one to have bought a car through a finance company. Fortunately I finished paying for it fourteen months ago. But a great many persons in Canada will lose everything because they cannot make their payments.

Having consulted with the Social Credit group and for the reasons that I have just mentioned, and in order to bring into line the finance companies which take advantage of the small wage earner, I can say that we are going to vote for Bill C-7.

Mr. Speaker, I realize, of course, that the matter we are discussing will not quicken the hearts of many Canadians but I do agree that it has very important implications for what I might call a credit cushioned society. I think the hon. member for Kootenay East is naive when he suggests to us that all those sellers who are anxious to extend credit investigate the people to whom they are advancing credit. This has not been my experience. I think it is one of the deplorable aspects of today's commercial practice that the ability of the purchaser to repay is all too often forgotten.
Having said that, I think that as a lawyer I must admit that on many occasions the commercial statutes of the provinces and of this parliament do not in any way keep pace with the facts of commercial life. I suggest that the amendment to the Bankruptcy Act which has been introduced in another place satisfies many of the provisions of Bill No. C-7 now before us. I share the views of the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka about the constitutional problem involved in this bill. I am not one of those who worship at the altar of provincial rights but on the other hand I do not think this house should walk into a constitutional problem when we have been forewarned about it.
I also feel, as has been said by the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka, that the grave deficiency in the present bill is that a wage earner-apparently the bill is intended to include only wage earners-must make an assignment before this legislation becomes effective. In other words, he must go bankrupt. This is a tragic thing. As I understand it, he could not even be sent to the other place if he was a bankrupt, at least an undischarged one, and we can think of many other disabilities that might face him. Not the least of these is the disability of being known as a bankrupt.
I think this is a grave deficiency in the bill before us. I suggest that the bill introduced require a longer period than that normally

in the other place makes no such drastic provision and therefore it would be well if we waited for the progress of that bill from the other place to this place.
(Translation):

Mr. Speaker, I am sure that the reasons which led the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow) to introduce this bill are praiseworthy.
Like the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Gregoire), I must say that even if all salesmen do not act that way, some high-pressure salesmen nowadays do not even take the trouble of inquiring about a person's income before they sell him all kinds of merchandise. We have often met people who have gone bankrupt after signing contracts with such companies.
We must examine this question in the light of those facts, but I feel that the bill introduced by the hon. member for Winnipeg North is somewhat of a replica of the legislation presently under consideration in the Senate. In fact, I had the opportunity of discussing a similar bill with high officials of the government and they referred me to the bill which is before the Senate at present. I have read and re-read that bill, and I really think we should wait until Bill S-2 is passed in order to determine whether it really protects our fellow citizens, wage earners or others in the province of Quebec and in the other provinces of Canada. And if later we, the representatives of the people, both of the wage earners and farmers, find out that that bill does not provide enough protection to wage earners or farmers, it will then be up to us to introduce again in the house a measure to amend that bill, a measure which certainly will be adopted.
As I was saying a moment ago, Mr. Speaker, the reasons which have led the hon. member for Winnipeg North to introduce this measure are good and commendable. On the other hand, I am of the opinion that all members must clearly express their opinion on this bill, in order that we may introduce the best possible measures to protect our wage earners, our farmers and the people in general.
Besides, I noticed that the hon. member for Lapointe agrees wholeheartedly with me when he talks of those high pressure salesmen who, through certain finance companies, go around selling sewing machines, aluminum windows or what have you. The discussion could go on for hours and hours as to why the workers buy these machines or those different articles. However, we could also remind them that when they purchase
Bankruptcy Act
some article, when they sign a contract, they have to pay for it. This does not mean, obviously, that these people are always responsible for those purchases, for too often, the salesmen have tried to lure the customers with what they claim are fine things but which, in fact, are not.
Mr. Speaker, I am in favour of the principle of the bill, but I think we should wait and see what will happen to the bill which is before the other place, in order to be able to see whether there is anything wrong with it and then propose amendments which would certainly benefit the whole country.

Mr. Speaker, I shall be brief as I do not want to speak until six o'clock.
I should like to point out, however, that the principle of the bill now before us should not be discussed by this house for the good reason that it raises a point of civil law which, in my humble opinion, comes essentially within provincial jurisdiction. Besides, as was stated earlier, the province of Quebec has assumed its responsibilities with regard to the problem caused by the insolvency of the small wage earners.
Therefore, under the pretext that this bill could be related to the Bankruptcy Act, we should not connect to that legislation measures of all kinds which would actually be appended to an act of an exceptional nature, because the Bankruptcy Act is an exception to the general rule providing that all matters of civil law come essentially under provincial jurisdiction.
In concluding, Mr. Speaker, I state once again that under the British North America Act, this matter falls strictly within the competence of the provinces and should not be considered by this house.

Mr. Speaker, members have talked about salesmen, bankrupt people, all sorts of things.
I am a salesman myself, maybe not the kind of high pressure salesman referred to, but selling has been my profession for 25 years.
I have seen all sorts of things in my life. So I have not much sympathy for certain finance companies, because I have seen so many people robbed by them in a masterful way.
Hear, hear.

I will refer to a case which may seem somewhat ridiculous. When I was

Bankruptcy Act
working for a big company in the province of Quebec which had sold goods to a certain person, with note after note, I remember that the goods were completely worn out after ten years and the customer still owed more than at the time he purchased the goods.
Legal proceedings are taken against those people. On the other hand, we must admit that some public trustees press people into declaring bankruptcy, when the amount involved is only some $300 or $400, thus freezing their credit, reflecting on their good name and causing them a lot of trouble practically for the rest of their lives.
Earlier today, I heard two hon. members state that there always were lawyers to protect those people. Of course, those lawyers are members of a very distinguished profession, but we should keep in mind that the business of those gentlemen is said to have prospered only during the depression, which means that a good many people had accounts to collect.
In all those matters, it is not so much the individual who is to blame, because, on the television as well as on the radio, he is told all day long: ladies and gentlemen, if you want to be happy, you must have this, and you must have that.
On the other hand, if we were to object too much to those people buying on instalments what they have to buy now and if they were to stop buying, we would really And ourselves living in a period of austerity. You can be sure that that situation would be worse than the former, because the manufacturers would stop producing.
There is something wrong and the house must take the matter under discussion and consider it in the interest of the Canadian people.

In rising to speak oh this particular bill, Mr. Speaker, I must say that while I agree with the greater part of the principles behind the bill, there are a few objections that I should like to point out in the short time remaining. The first objection is that this bill is mainly for wage earners. It makes no provision for the small farmer or other individuals who could not rightfully be classed as wage earners.
