speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order; the hour appointed for private members' business having expired, the house will now revert to the business that was interrupted at five o'clock.

The house resumed consideration in committee of Bill No. C-63, to amend the Export Credits Insurance Act-Mr. Hees-Mr. Paul in the chair.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 8 p.m.
On clause 3-Power to lend or guarantee, etc.

Mr. Chairman, I had occasion to suggest to the minister yesterday that the additional sum of $200 million might more properly be applied to the regular business of the corporation rather than the section 21 business; namely, the section 14 type of business rather than section 21. Could the minister explain why the order in council procedure has been chosen rather than giving effect to the remarks that have been made as to the highly satisfactory degree of performance of this corporation irt the past, its ability to transact business and the desire of the government to avoid red tape, including the passing of orders in council. All these arguments lead to increasing the section 14 authorization rather than section 21.

Mr. Chairman, I am glad to answer that question. Under section 14, which is the section under which regular business is transacted, there is the $200 million available to the corporation which is considered by the corporation to be quite sufficient to handle the regular business which it transacts, because as the hon. member will realize, this is regular, short term business and the amount of money used at any one time to provide this insurance is continually revolving as transactions become completed in a relatively short space of time. There is no need, in the opinion of either the corporation or the government, to increase the amount of money available to allow the corporation to carry out all of the regular insurance business it is called upon to carry out.
However, there is a considerable increase throughout the trading world in the type of transaction which section 21(a) is called upon to handle; that is, large transactions which

required under section 14. There are two reasons we require an enlargement of the amount of money available to insure this kind of transaction. First of all, these transactions are usually very large ones covering shipments of wheat, grains, machinery, industrial raw materials, and so on, and governments, particularly those of the United States and Great Britain, and also governments such as those of Germany, France and other industrialized countries, are using this kind of special, large scale insurance on a longer than normal term to make it possible for their exporters to obtain this kind of business in the world market. We are faced with the alternative of either meeting the terms which are made available to exporters in these other countries, or forgoing the business.
As the hon. member knows very well, the trading world of today is becoming an increasingly competitive market place and this government believes it is necessary to make available the kind of insurance that section 21 makes possible in order to obtain for Canada the large scale orders which otherwise could not be obtained for this country, orders which provide not only revenue for the country but a great deal of additional employment for Canadians and also enable Canada, like any other country, to better meet its international payments.

Mr. Chairman, if I might ask a further, supplementary question. As I understand it, sections 14 and 21 do not make any distinction in regard to term, upon which the minister appears to be dwelling; that is, that section 21 business is a different term business. As I recollect, the term is not mentioned in section 14.

Mr. Chairman, under section 14 the corporation handles all business which in the normal trading world of today is considered normal business. In other words, there is a recognized period of completion of a transaction for practically every type of commodity, a period during which it is reasonable to expect that the transaction for that particular type of commodity should be completed.
When requests are made to the corporation for insurance to cover a normal period at a normal rate of charge for that service, the corporation covers those transactions on its own under the authority provided it in section 14. But if the terms requested by the exporter in order to meet the competition from foreign countries are such that the directors of the corporation consider that such business is not normal business, it is of a longer period than that which would normally be allowed for the completion of the transaction; or if it is
Export Credits Insurance Act for an amount of money which is considered to be abnormal compared with what is considered normal for a single transaction for that type of business, then the corporation appeals to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, to the governor in council, for authorization by the governor in council to insure that extra large transaction for an extra long term.

Now that we have come to the third section of the proposed amendments I should like to direct two questions to the attention of the minister. Last Friday the hon. member for Leeds made two statements in speaking on this measure, and one of them got some small notice in the press. The first was that the function of this legislation has changed over a period of time from being primarily an insurance function to being primarily a banking function. The second statement was to the effect that we were now publicly subsidizing a financing operation.
I have read the act, together with the proposed amendments, with some care and it does not seem to me that the amendments in any way increased the lending function of the corporation. Further, neither in the original act nor in any subsequent amendment can I find any reference to any subsidy. I should like the minister to tell me, if he can, whether or not this is the case.

Yes, I am glad to answer those two questions. Whereas the function of the corporation has changed somewhat due to the addition of section 21(a), it is still primarily that of an insurance corporation with financing added by the section I have mentioned. However, I stress that the primary function of the corporation is insurance. For example, if this bill passes the house, and I hope it will, there will be $600 million devoted to the insurance function and $300 million to the financing function.
The hon. member also asked whether the operation of the corporation subsidized the Department of Finance or the government. The answer is that it does not. As I said in my opening remarks on Friday, these operations, whether they involve insurance or financing, cost the taxpayers of Canada not one penny. The premiums for insurance and the interest charges for financing are fixed as far as possible on a break even basis, the object being that the corporation should neither make nor lose money. Naturally, in the interest of the taxpayers we tend to be on the black side of the ledger and, if anything, there is a slight profit made. But, as I said in answer to a question asked earlier in this debate, the profit over the period since

Export Credits Insurance Act the corporation began operating 17 years ago amounts to only one fifth of 1 per cent. Thus I believe all hon. members will agree that the corporation operates on a break even basis and does not subsidize the government in any way.

I think the committee has benefited greatly tonight from the frank statement by the minister that this legislation is designed primarily to reach into foreign markets for Canadian goods in a strongly competitive world. I believe everyone agrees that the world today has come to a point where competition is extremely brutal. I was assured by a gentleman from Europe about a month ago that his firm had retained a bloc of business in Europe by investing in Florida real estate and owning several thousand bales of United States cotton. This sort of thing is increasing around the world and the minister is to be commended for pointing out to the committee that this is one of the techniques being used by foreign countries and now being adopted by ourselves to get Canadian goods into markets where they might not otherwise go.
I think, however, that the committee is entitled to have from the minister a series of answers to questions relating to the past experience to the corporation, because I note that the amendment provides for an extension into a number of activities not normally associated with a crown corporation or with this type of corporation.
I note that subsection (2) of section 21(a) empowers the corporation to lend money to an importer on the security of an instrument given by an importer in respect to an export transaction. It also extends to the corporation the right to purchase a guaranteed instrument or to lend money to the holder of a guaranteed instrument, or to sell to any person a guaranteed instrument. This means, I suggest to the minister, that the corporation is getting into that ancient but honest business of factoring, if I may use the term, and this is new to a corporation of this kind. I note that the powers given to the corporation in the past are not unlike those to which the amendment addresses itself, because formerly the corporation when authorized by the governor in council could guarantee by a proper endorsement or otherwise the payment of an instrument, or it could purchase a guaranteed instrument or lend money to the holder of such an instrument. I think the minister might well tell the committee what has been the experience in the past in this area of operations and I should also like to know where in the trading of these instruments he hopes the corporation will find a free and competitive market, because it would
fMr. Hees.]
seem to me they would be handled by banking institutions or discount houses rather than offered freely to the public. I am not suggesting that the corporation which trades in these instruments becomes the prisoner of the export credits corporation but I do fear a situation where, due to the unusual nature of the instrument, the corporation might become the prisoner of the two or three institutions who would trade in them.
Earlier, the minister replied to the hon. member for Rosedale and suggested that while the transactions had been carried out with banking institutions it might be the intention of the corporation to offer these instruments freely. I ask the hon. gentleman in connection with the items in the annual report listed under section 21(a) and involving, I think, the lending of some $41 million to four different countries, or corporations in those countries, if there is any experience in connection with the handling of these bonds or commitments by the countries concerned which he thinks would be profitable for the committee to know. I notice that the interest rate is listed at 6 per cent. Have these bonds been sold and if so were they sold at a discount?
I have listed a number of questions of the minister and I want to thank him for telling the committee tonight very frankly that this is a very competitive world and that this is one of the weapons we are using to fight it. The minister might also tell us the reason for the advance of the insurance rate under section 14 from 88 cents per $100 in 1954 to the average of this last year of about $1.35 per $100.

Mr. Chairman, in answer to the last question I am advised that the rate has gone down from 88 cents to less than 66 cents on the business done under section 14. I am advised that the hon. member for Vancouver South is referring to the business done under section 21, under which section the length of term of the transactions has been increasing. It has been necessary to allow this increase in the rate and the length of term in order to meet terms made available to their exporters by other governments. I do hope the hon. member understands what I mean. In reply to the question before that, the answer is that we have not sold any paper whatsoever. The reason why we ask for the right to adopt these new techniques of selling paper and of allowing loans to be made on paper which is bought is because this is the practice which has worked out well for the export-import bank of the United States and the export credits guarantee department of Great Britain. They have found that the techniques for which we are asking in this legislation have worked well for them. We have the same kind of operation here, and

are therefore asking parliament to give the Export Credits Insurance Corporation of Canada the right to operate in the same way.

Mr. Chairman, this afternoon the minister assured the hon. member for Danforth that the proposed subsection (2) of section 21(a) empowered the corporation to lend money to the government of a foreign country. This, of course, was something that we were most anxious to know and delighted to hear; but in view of the fact that when section 21(a) was first brought into existence a year ago it contained a definition of "importer" which said that an importer means "a person carrying on business or other activities outside Canada", can the minister assure the house that he has been advised by those responsible for giving such opinion to the corporation and to his department that a government of a foreign country is included within the definition of "importer" contained in the act when it was amended last year? That is when section 21(a) was first inserted into the act. If the minister is able to assure us that that is so, then there can be no problem; but if he cannot, then an amendment might be required.
Mr. Chairman, as I mentioned earlier in this debate the importer may be either a private firm or a department of a foreign government. Does that answer the hon. member's question?

Well, Mr. Chairman, I and the other hon. members who sit in this corner would be most happy if we could be assured that a legal opinion had been given to the minister to the effect that section 21(a)(1)(c) of the Export Credits Insurance Act in fact included the government of a foreign nation within the meaning of "importer". Our concern is that the minister might find himself, after the legislation presently before the committee has gone through, in the position where he may be advised that the corporation in fact has no legal power to make a loan to the government of a foreign nation. Because paragraph (c) of the amendment brought into the act last year says that an importer means a person carrying on business or other activities outside Canada. For some of us it may seem unlikely that a person, as those words are used in the act, is meant to include the government of a foreign country. Some of us might be led to the view that the words "a person" were designed only to cover persons outside Canada wishing to purchase exports and wishing to obtain loans from Canada. That is the difficulty that some of us feel. We are not trying to hold matters up; we just want to make sure that the government has every legal power at its command to enable it to carry out the provisions of the act.
Export Credits Insurance Act

Mr. Chairman, I appreciate very much the concern of the hon. member about this matter, and I wish to assure him that the corporation has the right to deal directly with the government, and has been doing so during the past year. If he would look at the annual report of the Export Credits Insurance Corporation, page 13 lists a number of transactions carried out under section 21(a) in various countries. All of those transactions have either been carried out directly with the government of the country concerned or guaranteed by that government.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the minister two questions arising out of his reply to the question put by the hon. member for Simcoe North. If I understood the minister correctly, he said that the corporation conducted affairs in such a way as to stay in the black and not be a charge to the taxpayers. However, I also gathered that the operations were conducted so as not to make any exorbitant profit. My two questions are these. Does the corporation pay income tax and, if so, how much income tax was paid last year?
Mr. Chairman, the answer to the first question is yes, the corporation does pay income tax; and last year the corporation paid $740,427 in income tax.

Mr. Chairman, this would seem to be good legislation if wisely and efficiently administered, and in respect to administration I should like to ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce if under this third amendment the conditions of approval of an export contract have been determined as yet. That is, the conditions of the contract and approval of the contract. If so, are they analogous to the United States export-import bank requirements of which he spoke? If they are, where can we see the catalogue?
Mr. Chairman, if the hon. member had been in the committee last night he would not have asked the question, because I answered it then.
I was here but that was in respect of the guarantees.

In order to clear the situation up may I inquire whether these regulations apply to the third amendment similarly to the way in which he said they applied to the guarantees? Is that what I am given to understand?

Yes.
Clause 3 agreed to.

Title agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman, and through you, of course, the members of the committee. There has been an increase in lending each year, which can be followed from the chart, from an annual total of about $12 million in 1956 to almost $69 million in 1961. During the current year there is a further increase in loans of about 22 per cent and the volume of loans is expected to exceed $80 million by the end of the year. I would suggest that is a considerable record.
[The Deputy Chairman.]
Although I am sure no one can seriously question the success of our credit program, the government has been examining the legislation to see if the Farm Credit Corporation can play a larger role in our rapidly developing agricultural program. It will be recalled that when the Farm Credit Act was being considered in committee on June 29, 1959 it was stated, as found in Hansard, page 5256, that this government would be prepared to modify the credit program established under the new

act if experience showed that this was necessary for the improvement of farm family living, farm operating and farm purchase. The bill now being proposed is intended to fulfil that undertaking.
Some of the proposals which are advanced in this bill are intended to correct some minor anomalies in the act and to remove some restrictions which have been found by experience to be unnecessary. There are other proposals, however, which are more fundamental in nature. For example, an examination of the loans made in each of the areas in Canada will reveal in general a very good record but there are areas which in my opinion are not making full use of this very fine legislation. I refer to some of the eastern counties of Ontario, the provinces of Quebec and British Columbia and the Atlantic provinces. Some of these amendments are therefore intended to broaden the credit program so that farmers will have greater latitude in the use of the money they borrow.
Amendments are proposed which will permit the corporation to lend money, for example, to make improvements to any part of the land the farmer is operating including land, such as that on long term lease, which is not covered by the mortgage to the corporation. Another amendment will permit the corporation to lend money to pay the farmer's operating and living costs during the early period of his loan while he is developing his farm to a self-supporting level or during a transitional period when he is changing from one type of enterprise to another and temporarily has very little farm income.
It will interest many members to know that these amendments are planned to help the farmer to develop non-agricultural enterprises on his farm, such as camping grounds, tourist cabins or cottages and so on, if he can make more profitable use of his land resources in this way. These latter proposals obviously broaden the role of the Farm Credit Corporation in the field of agricultural adjustment. They will make it possible for the corporation to provide much greater support to our program of agricultural rehabilitation and development. This bill, together with amendments to farm credit regulations which are at present under consideration, will open the door for closer co-ordination of the Farm Credit Corporation and the ARDA administration and will mark a new milestone in our attack upon the problem of the low income of an important segment of our farming population.
Mr. Chairman, I commend this legislation to the committee.

speechtext: In this past year; the record in one year.

maintopic: TOTAL ANNUAL LOAN DISBURSEMENTS IN MILLIONS OF DOLLARS 20-YEAR TREND
speechtext: One year?

maintopic: TOTAL ANNUAL LOAN DISBURSEMENTS IN MILLIONS OF DOLLARS 20-YEAR TREND
speechtext:
One year. In one year 55 per cent were rejected; 55 per cent did not get anything. I suggest to hon. members opposite -and I know what a number of them want because I have been talking to them personally; they are interested in seeing this program expanded-that a 55 per cent rejection is too high, there is something wrong, and whatever is wrong should be corrected. I do not think it is too hard to find out what is wrong. The mistake was made when this legislation was brought in by the present government in 1959. It is a mistake which has been continued, and it is a mistake which has been set forth in black and white. Let no one misunderstand it. I have in my hand a document called "Farm Credit Corporation Lending Policy for 1961". On page 1, this is what it says in part:
While not explicitly stated, this thinking is implied in the legislation and in the regulations made under it, and was very well expressed by the Minister of Agriculture when he defined the object of the legislation as follows:
This is the object-this is in quotation marks:
"To assist Canadian farmers in the voluntary reorganization of their industry into economic family farm units, each of which will be of sufficient size to produce, under the operation of the owner, the farm income necessary to meet all operating and maintenance costs, provide an adequate livelihood for the owner-operator and his dependents, and retire any required credit, with interest, within an appropriate term."
Here is what they say to the farmer: When you receive this loan, will you be in possession of an economic family farm unit of a sufficient size to produce an income for the family, to provide an adequate livelihood and to retire your debt with interest? This means that if a small farmer comes in and asks for a small loan the people administering this legislation say: will this small loan which the farmer is requesting, together with the property he now has, make his farm into an

economic unit so that he can have a good standard of living and retire his debts? Often they say: no, it is not enough-which is probably true-and instead of providing this small farmer with a relatively small loan to improve his position they say: until you get a bigger farm so that you can take a bigger loan we shall not give you anything at all. That is the policy. That is the basis upon which the whole thing is done. So a farmer in the Gatineau valley asks for a loan, and they say: "Well, you did not make much money last year and you do not have much property. You only want a small loan. We shall not give you one; you are a poor risk". That is the attitude. That must be the reason. I do not know any other. Yet the record of repayment shows that the small farmer as well as the large farmer has an excellent credit record, and the corporation has lost practically no money in the period of its operations.
The annual report was given to us a little while ago, and what did it say about losses? Well, the farmers did not pay some money, so they had to write off loans of- how much?-of $12,496 in one year, with well over $200 million outstanding. Still, there was a loss of $978,915. Why? Because this government has brought interest rates so high that the corporation cannot operate without losses on the basis of a 5 per cent interest charge. The farmers have been a good risk. The farmers have paid their debts. But the government, through its failures, is responsible for the high interest rates in the country. I do not hold the Minister of Agriculture individually responsible for this; he does not always agree with his colleagues in many important ways. However, the losses have occurred not because the farmers were poor risks but because this government was a poor risk.
I have outlined what they say to a farmer when he comes in for a loan, and I have done so on the basis of the minister's own statement. If that needs underlining-and I really do not see why it should-all one needs to do is to quote from the farm credit regulations themselves. This is what they say:
12(1). No loan shall be made on the security of farm land that is not part of a farm unit of sufficient size to produce, under the operation of the applicant, crops and fodder which, whether fed to livestock with or without normal purchased feed supplements-
It does not matter if he purchases a lot of western feed grain; that is not taken into account.
-marketed directly or both, will produce revenue sufficient to

(i)	pay the cost of operating and maintenance of the farm unit,
(ii)	provide a livelihood for the applicant-
Then, when a farmer comes in and has a talk with them, before they take his $50, they have a report made out and there is a question asked there of the officer of the corporation: "Does it appear the enterprise will qualify under regulation 12(1)?" That is the regulation I have just quoted. Thus, by arbitrary action, as stated by the minister and by the regulations themselves, a large proportion of the agricultural producers of this country are barred from deriving any benefit whatsoever under this legislation, and the proportion barred is relatively higher in the eastern provinces.
What kind of regulations should there be? I will suggest some changes in this regard to the minister, if I may. I would suggest that instead of the statement which the hon. gentleman himself has used it should read something like this: "This money shall be such as to aid farmers in the voluntary reorganization of their industry into more economic family farm units, each of which, under the operation of the owner, will meet all operation and maintenance costs, retire any credit with interest within an appropriate term and, with the credit obtained from the corporation, provide a more adequate livelihood for the owner operator and his dependents. In other words, will the loan improve the farmer's position-not whether it will make up an economic unit. This is the basis upon which we suggest, from this side, the whole act should be operated. The test should be: will it help an individual applicant to improve his position, not whether it would give him an economic unit. I say this because how can a small farmer ever get an economic unit if he is not to be allowed the credit in stages which would help him to improve his business?
I would like to suggest, now, on behalf of the official opposition that this legislation should be referred to the standing committee on agriculture and colonization. The minister brags about this legislation. That is fine. Let us have the committee meet; let us have the officials from the department come before the committee. Let us hear evidence from the minister. Let the officials deal with some of the statements which have been made this afternoon and let us see how, together, we as members of parliament on this committee can make suggestions to improve the operation of this act. We should like to have the agricultural committee meet to consider certain suggestions and proposals. These would be designed to increase the number
Farm Credit Act
of loans in all parts of Canada with particular emphasis on increasing the number of loans in those areas where they are in relatively small numbers at the present time. We should also consider what further action is required both by regulation and by administrative decision to make more loans available to low income farmers.
We would suggest that there should be amendments to the legislation and to the regulations to make it possible to lend money on a poultry operation as well as a livestock operation. We would suggest to the minister that the definition of "livestock" should be extended to include not only cattle, sheep and hogs but also horses. I do not see any reason why a farmer who raises horses for the ranching country and for use in the farming industry should be barred from getting credit for this part of his operations. In other words, the scope of the act should be extended to provide a broader definition of the word "livestock" and also to include poultry enterprises within the farming operation. We would ask that consideration be given either to the complete removal of the $50 deterrent or to a very substantial reduction in this deterrent. A $50 bar is a substantial one which should not stand in the Way of small income earners who are obtaining a loan. We would also suggest that under this legislation consideration should be given to providing loans for farm housing on the security of the house, and a very small amount of property immediately surrounding the house, and that the farmer should not be required to tie up his whole operation in order to get decent living quarters for his family or his hirelings.

Mr. Chairman, I have just a few more suggestions to make. The minister said in his statement that consideration should be given to working this legislation in with the ARDA program. It might have been the case that certain amendments would be necessary to provide moneys to producers on a group basis who wished to take part in any ARDA program. I would have put much greater emphasis on this a few days ago, but after the announcement of the minister that

Farm Credit Act
the ARDA program is going to be composed of a number of pilot projects and research over a three year period, the need for this kind of proposal may not be as great as I had anticipated. Another suggestion we would make is that consideration be given under this legislation, or by some other action if it seemed more appropriate, to provide emergency or disaster loans to agricultural producers who suffered tremendous losses because of storms, floods, or other acts of God. There was a tremendous storm on the coast of British Columbia recently, and this merely suggests that this kind of . proposal has great merit. It is not crop insurance. It does not go that far; it is a moderate suggestion. It is asking for just this, that farmers who suffer tremendous losses and who lose a large part of their assets because of an act of nature should be eligible for an emergency or disaster loan without interest for a period of time until they have had some time to rehabilitate their business. We further suggest that under this act there should be further emphasis on research and an expansion of the work of this corporation.
Lastly, Mr. Chairman, we would suggest that the amount involved at this time, even under the minister's own terms, does not seem to be a sufficient amount of money except for a brief period of time. This measure means an increase in available funds of $100 million. The minister said that he hopes this year that there may be loans totalling $80 million, and it would seem to me to be a great encouragement to the Farm Credit Corporation if we were to provide sufficient funds for a two year or a three year operation so that their funds would not be of an order which would last probably for only 16 or 18 months. Mr. Chairman, no matter where hon. members sit in this house, no matter to which party hon. members may belong, I believe the members who represent agricultural communities are interested in this legislation and would like to see improvements made. We suggest to the Minister of Agriculture and to this committee that this legislation should be referred to the committee on agriculture, where the important proposals that we have put forward may be considered, and we express the hope that these recommendations will be brought back from the committee and put in legislative form.

maintopic: TOTAL ANNUAL LOAN DISBURSEMENTS IN MILLIONS OF DOLLARS 20-YEAR TREND
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I do not know why the Minister of Agriculture should wish to give me all this prominence and publicity by asking that question; I do not know what it does for him, I am sure. All I can say to the Minister of Agriculture is that I have put forward on behalf of the Liberal party some suggestions that he would be very wise to consider in the interests of this country.

maintopic: TOTAL ANNUAL LOAN DISBURSEMENTS IN MILLIONS OF DOLLARS 20-YEAR TREND
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think that the hon. member for Assiniboia should be congratulated for covering the complete scope of the Farm Credit Corporation. In fact, from the familiar way he speaks about it, I have almost come to the conclusion that he himself must be one of the 55 per cent who have tried to get a loan.

maintopic: TOTAL ANNUAL LOAN DISBURSEMENTS IN MILLIONS OF DOLLARS 20-YEAR TREND
speechtext: I think I should rise on a point of order. The hon. member well knows that members of parliament are not entitled to loans, and I am sure none of us has ever tried to get one.

speechtext: That does not bar one from trying.

maintopic: TOTAL ANNUAL LOAN DISBURSEMENTS IN MILLIONS OF DOLLARS 20-YEAR TREND
speechtext: Well, I have never tried; I have never even inquired.

maintopic: TOTAL ANNUAL LOAN DISBURSEMENTS IN MILLIONS OF DOLLARS 20-YEAR TREND
speechtext:
Nevertheless, the suggestion that this legislation should go before the agricultural committee is a good one, I think, as far as discussion is concerned, but I hardly see the need for that after having listened to this very eloquent discourse; and with all the propositions which have been put up, we should be able to get on with the legislation very quickly and probably manage to get through with it in less time than the one we have just been dealing with.
I speak only generally tonight, because I think it would be fairer to the minister to hear some of the suggestions and the amendments which he has said are coming before we go into too much pre-judging or discussion, which will arise as we proceed with this matter. But in principle we agree with this legislation. I think any of us who are familiar with the workings of the Farm Credit Corporation believe that the corporation does good work. That does not necessarily mean that it is the ultimate as far as what can be done, but nevertheless, in principle we support this measure. Again, in this regard there is one thought which comes to mind which concerns the finance which is behind this type of corporation. If our financial system were rearranged so as to be more in tune with the times and the conditions of which we are a part, then I believe the capital for this type of credit, rather than

coming from tax capital, ought to be available from private investment capital because it is productive capital.
However, at this point it is not necessary to discuss this matter in detail. In the present situation the Farm Credit Act performs a very useful function. In the practical application of the act there is one weakness with which I am personally familiar and it is concerned with the determining of what is an economic farm unit. In this regard I agree entirely with the remarks made by the hon. member for Assiniboia as to the need of making this credit available to the smaller farmer.
I believe that the basic outworking of the act, whether or not that is the intention, has been to assist the farmer to become an economic unit and the basis of this has been to enlarge the farms. There are many ways in which a farm can be made an economic unit other than by just expanding the area. I believe that in this regard particularly careful consideration should be given. I am thinking of other matters such as land levelling, the construction of storage facilities on the farm, root cellars and other types of storage; land clearing, drainage from low lying areas; and also the necessary improvements so far as productive capacity on a farm is concerned.
I say this principally because we are very much concerned about what is happening to the family farm unit. Year by year the number of farm units gets smaller and smaller. In this regard it is a very interesting sidelight to observe that we are gradually approaching the stage of industrial farming, whereas those countries in the world which have tried collective farming on a large scale, which is actually industrial farming, are coming back again to the smaller farm unit.
I think we must understand the place the family farm unit has in the hard core life which we know in Canada. I think that everything we deal with in this House of Commons as it relates to agriculture should be considered with the thought in mind that we must assist and protect the family farm unit as it attempts to survive, rather than to eliminate more and more of them and thus increase the size of that farm unit. I am acquainted with farmers who have been required to buy additional land in order to qualify as an economic unit when actually perhaps that had not been their basic need, and when the money could just as profitably have been applied to improving the land they already held.
The increase in the number of credits granted under the Farm Credit Corporation is commendable. As we listen to some of the suggestions the minister has for us, I hope they
Farm Credit Act
will be aimed at reaching those areas, particularly here in the eastern part of the country, where the participation on the part of the farmer has not been as widespread as it is in the west. Again I think the factor to which I have just been referring is very important, namely the recognition of the potential of improving the smaller farm units. We shall not talk more in that regard now. Another point which I think the hon. member for Assiniboia has already made concerns the assessment fee which is required and which is now $50. If this legislation is getting at a root problem in agriculture, surely the department and the minister should be considering the need of eliminating this fee altogether in order to encourage as many farmers as possible to take part in the Farm Credit Corporation.
I agree that the need for this legislation is more urgent now than it has been in any of the years past. Again, the decrease in the aggregate farm income which is running at a lower level today than it has run for a number of years, is a satisfactory indicator that there is a real basic need for this type of legislation.
On behalf of those in this corner of the house, I wish to assure the minister and the house that we are dealing with a positive piece of legislation and there is a certain amount of urgency. Again I say that, in so far as the over-all financial picture in the country is concerned, we should get on with it as quickly as possible.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I listened with interest to the minister's statement and as a result I am sure we all anticipate the bill and the revelations it will bring with respect to the proposed administrative changes.
I listened with interest to the hon. member for Assiniboia. While I agree with a great deal that he had to say, I am a bit under the impression that he is suffering from dyspepsia this evening. He referred to the minister's speech as flowery. I think that was really an exaggeration. Anyone who can call a succession of short statements linked together with statistics a flowery speech has rather an unusual understanding of the English language. I have a great respect for the minister, and I know of his wholehearted concern with this problem. However, he tread so softly across the grass of agricultural policy that I am almost reminded of Gray's "Elegy in a Country Churchyard".
The members of this group give their wholehearted support to this resolution. We recognize the value of the family unit in the maintenance of a democratic, diversified and sane society in Canada. I speak this evening as a countryman who has lived practically all his life in the country, and enjoyed it. I

Farm. Credit Act
would not live anywhere else if I could possibly help it. We recognize the need for this type of legislation in order to promote the development and improvement of the economic family farm unit. In recent years in some quarters we have heard a great deal, in some cases from agricultural economists, to the effect that the family farm is disappearing, that it is inefficient, that the countryside will soon be farmed by large corporate institutions and that the village hall, the village church and the village school will disappear. We in this group wholeheartedly disagree with that conception.

maintopic: TOTAL ANNUAL LOAN DISBURSEMENTS IN MILLIONS OF DOLLARS 20-YEAR TREND
speechtext: Will the hon. member name the economists who have said that?

maintopic: TOTAL ANNUAL LOAN DISBURSEMENTS IN MILLIONS OF DOLLARS 20-YEAR TREND
speechtext: No, I cannot remember the names of those economists. However, I remember reading several books which indicated that in the future farming would be undertaken in large units. I am sure the hon. gentleman has read some of that literature. I hope the hon. gentleman does not think I was referring to him just because I happened to look in that direction. He is guilty of many things in this house but I would never accuse him of that sort of thing. I am sure his heart is in the country.

maintopic: TOTAL ANNUAL LOAN DISBURSEMENTS IN MILLIONS OF DOLLARS 20-YEAR TREND
speechtext: What about the hon. member for Davenport?

maintopic: TOTAL ANNUAL LOAN DISBURSEMENTS IN MILLIONS OF DOLLARS 20-YEAR TREND

speechtext: Why?

maintopic: TOTAL ANNUAL LOAN DISBURSEMENTS IN MILLIONS OF DOLLARS 20-YEAR TREND

Because Brigadier Rutherford is a farmer at heart. He has had experience. He knows what raising cattle is, he knows what tilling the land is and when it comes to farm questions there is nothing like experience to enable one to speak with some common sense and with some authority. His services in his work as director of the Farm Credit Corporation have been recognized by farmers organizations, by many farmers with whom I have had the opportunity to discuss the matter and by farm papers across Canada, and I think we should pay a tribute to the services of a very capable civil servant who served his country well. Although he is now retired as director, his services are still available in an advisory capacity. I want to say that he has been succeeded by a gentleman who is equally interested in this question and is carrying on in his spirit, with his purpose and in his footsteps.
We talk about the decline of agriculture and the declining rural population, and we are talking like that when the need for farm products is growing daily with the increase in population in the world and not only with respect to our home market but with respect to the large populations of the world who need our agricultural production. To support my argument I want to quote briefly from page 17 of the report of the resources for tomorrow conference held in Montreal from October 23 to 28, 1961. There is a lot of good material in these reports. The thesis to which I wish to refer is headed "Demand Outlook for Canadian Agriculture" and reads in part as follows:
In Canada, over the next 20 years, we foresee a doubling of meat consumption and a 70 per cent increase in the total physical volume of foods consumed. At the same time we foresee an 80 per cent increase in the world demand for food, primarily for staple cereals. Therefore, while Canadian wheat exports may face some difficulty in the next five to ten years, the long term outlook is more hopeful. Since growth in domestic demand will shift Canadian agriculture strongly toward a livestock economy, there should be no great problem apart from short run variations in finding export outlets for the limited supplies of coarse grains which
Farm Credit Act
are surplus to domestic requirements. Agriculture can therefore expect, in the longer run, to enjoy the almost forgotten privileges of an expanding industry.
There is no question that that statement is a sound analysis of the opportunities for marketing in the years ahead. I have a few suggestions to make on behalf of this group with respect to this legislation. First of all, let me say that while the legislation is sound I would say it is not quite all we think it should be from the point of view of making progress in agriculture and I want to make a few suggestions as to the necessary things that should be added. We believe that a constructive over-all agricultural policy must be devised as a result of co-operation between the federal and provincial governments. There can be more of that done at these dominion-provincial agricultural conferences. We believe in a policy that provides for the promotion of farming as a way of life for increasing numbers, not decreasing numbers, and for the development of the economic family farm, which we have dealt with on numerous occasions. An economic family farm varies according to geography, the type of soil the farmer is cultivating, the crop he is growing and the circumstances under which he is farming. It is a variable; it changes all the way from the large grain farms of the prairies to the five acres of cherries or peaches that are grown by the fruit farmers in my district and from which they receive a gross income of about $6,000. This can be established very easily indeed.
Then, I believe there is another place where this legislation can be improved in its administration; possibly the regulations require amendment. There was something in what the hon. member for Assiniboia had to say in respect of the smaller farms. I would say there is an opportunity for the development of what I call the modest maintenance farm for those who find satisfaction and happiness living under rural circumstances. We are so inclined to think everybody wants to make money. I have hundreds of farmers of this type in my constituency whose material standard of living is lower than the average of many, but whose real standard of living is quite high because of the circumstances under which they live.

maintopic: TOTAL ANNUAL LOAN DISBURSEMENTS IN MILLIONS OF DOLLARS 20-YEAR TREND
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member if the Freedomites live in his constituency?

maintopic: TOTAL ANNUAL LOAN DISBURSEMENTS IN MILLIONS OF DOLLARS 20-YEAR TREND
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman has not been reading the newspapers recently. I am glad to report that they are now living in the constituency of the hon. member for Fraser Valley.
I say there are a good many of these people who live on small farms, who produce many of their own requirements, and have sufficient

Farm Credit Act
to buy the things they need. They are quite happy living modestly. In many cases they have nice homes, lawns, gardens, good libraries and things of that sort. This type of modest maintenance farm should receive some consideration in this type of legislation. As I say, I have hundreds of people of this type in my constituency who farm in this way, and who are not concerned with money. They simply want to enjoy the country in which they live. I want to say that I represent the garden of Eden in more than one sense. It is geographically beautiful; and then we have other features that were found in the garden of Eden in the early days. I do suggest that consideration should be given to what I call the modest maintenance farm, the people who enjoy this type of life and who are really happy.

maintopic: TOTAL ANNUAL LOAN DISBURSEMENTS IN MILLIONS OF DOLLARS 20-YEAR TREND
speechtext: Come over and join us.

maintopic: TOTAL ANNUAL LOAN DISBURSEMENTS IN MILLIONS OF DOLLARS 20-YEAR TREND
speechtext:
I can see that I am making converts wholesale amongst the Social Credit members. It is wonderful to see how they change once they come here.
Then, there is another type of farm that should receive some consideration and that is the part time farm related to industry, such as the tree farm. This type of farming is growing. The industrial worker can come home, and because of the equipment that is available today he can raise 3,000 chickens or farm four or five acres of orchard. I think this part time farming should be encouraged and the legislation should give some consideration to this type of farming. The more Canadians you keep close to the soil, the safer Canada will be.
Then, there should be a program to provide research into the social and economic problems of agriculture. I should like to quote from a statement to the federal-provincial agricultural conference by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture on this question. I quote:
The Canadian Federation of Agriculture is increasingly convinced of the urgent need for increased and more effective independent research into the economic and social problems of agriculture. It fully supports the findings of the Winnipeg national conference on farm policy research, and in particular the view that there is a great need for research into the effects and implications of agricultural policies, and into the probable effects and implications of policy alternatives which are open to us.
I think there could be considerable research in that direction. So far as production is concerned, we are getting along fairly well. So far as marketing is concerned, I think a good job has been done. However, I feel we need more research into the economic and social problems of various

types of agriculture, and how federal and provincial governments can be of assistance in meeting these problems.
I believe also we have to have an agriculture policy that provides for a complete revision of the tax policies at provincial and municipal levels. I know that is not within the compass of the federal government. I believe this is something that can be worked out at dominion-provincial conferences on agriculture. This is a very serious problem to the farmers all across Canada, the question of provincial and municipal taxes. I think there is a great deal that can be done to assist the development of the farm and the extension of rural life by a change in our agricultural taxation policy.
I think there is need for a policy to provide for further studies into all aspects of financing the family farm, the modest maintenance farm and the part time farmers, as I would call them. In that connection, I want to quote again from this conservation bible of mine, the report of the resources for tomorrow conference. This is a brief paragraph which is found on page 114. It is headed "Financing the farm firm" and states:
It is very difficult to obtain a comprehensive picture of the problems associated with the current capital and credit position of Canadian farmers. A greater quantity of credit is now available to farmers as a result of recent federal and provincial credit legislation. For the present it would appear that the available credit is reasonably adequate for the development of efficient family farm units in Canada. However, several problems need to be anticipated from the standpoint of financing the farm firm of the future. Consideration needs to be given to the following areas:
(a)	Beginning farmers: Studies need to be carried out to discover how the present credit legislation applies to the beginning farmer. Considerable research needs to be devoted to the area of supervised credit, and how far the public credit agencies should go in substituting supervision for equity collateral for the beginning farmer.
(b)	Use of credit consistent with the required adjustments of the agriculture industry. For example, studies might be initiated to examine the problems associated with the attempt by the lending agencies to lay a more positive role in the use of credit in agriculture.
(c)	Study needs to be devoted to the possibilities of tenancy as a method of obtaining much needed sources of long term capital in agriculture.
(d)	Steps need to be taken to see that more liberal credit policies are not capitalized into higher land values.
(e)	A comprehensive study is needed to examine the problems associated with, and the continued feasibility of, the farm operator accumulating the full value of the farm assets once every generation.
(f)	Study needs to be given to the problems and possibilities of adopting the share capital method of financing the agricultural industry consistent with the ideal of the family farm.

Our policy is one of planning which permits co-operation between federal

and provincial governments, farmers and farm organizations. You note, Mr. Chairman, although we suffer temporarily from the disability of a Progressive Conservative government, we have much to be grateful for in this country. I think we have always got to remember this: There are many things that should be done for a great number of Canadians, but we should be grateful that we are Canadians, live in Canada and have opportunities.
I am going to tell you a story before I conclude. When I was in Britain-

I shall finish in three minutes. When I was in Britain I met an old lady, 75 years of age and I talked with her. I told her that I admired her. She said, "Mr. Herridge, I was born in this street and I am dying in this street, and no blooming Hitler will ever blow me out." Do you know, sir, that from the time I was a girl, up to the battle of Britain I had to take medicine for my bowels. I have never had to take any since".

Mr. Chairman, in concluding may I say that the dear old lady said to me, "Do you know how I am showing my gratitude. I have been participating in government ever since. I am doing all I can to make things better for the folk on our street".
I think we can learn a lesson from that old lady. We have much to be grateful for. We have a duty and a responsibility to promote farming as a way of life, to promote the restoration of rural Canada to its former greatness and its position in Canadian society. We want a policy that provides purpose and opportunity for participation, planning by governments, co-operation among farmers and community organization, all based on the initiative and virtues of farm folk.
Progress reported.
